chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.note: This introductory unit begins with a compact cosmogonic survey (eternal separation, assault of Darkness, First Man, Living Spirit’s construction, Third Ambassador, final fire and binding) in an impersonal, cosmological voice—likely preserving the oldest teaching substrate. After this, the register pivots sharply into self-authorization (Mani’s books), institutional/audience address, and comparative-apostolic polemic (Jesus/Zarathustra/Buddha), with strong late pastoral/application drift and a detected editorial extension.

chapters.title: Concerning the Ad[vent] of the Apostle.
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by later layers: dialogue framing, apostolic-succession instruction, and extensive New Testament-derived narrative (Jesus, Judas, Paul, Paraclete sayings). The only recoverable correspondential/cosmological substrate appears as brief embedded summaries of mysteries (Depths/Heights; Light/Darkness; construction of the Ships; purification mechanics; Adam myth), preserved inside Mani-autobiographical revelation rhetoric.

chapters.title: The Second, concerning the Parable of the Tree.
chapters.note: The chapter opens in a Gospel-driven dialogue frame (Q&A + explicit Gospel citation) and then digresses into NT exempla (Judas/Paul) and sectarian polemic. The oldest teaching substrate emerges most clearly from ¶11 onward in systematic five-fold correspondences (five limbs/mental qualities mapped to cosmic hypostases and ships) and in the negative five-fold of the bad tree culminating in the "lump" and Darkness. Two strong institutional grafts occur as editorial seams (¶13, ¶16), where the correspondential pattern is extended to the holy church/catechumens/alms.

chapters.title: The Interpretation of Happiness, Wisdom and Power; what they signify.
chapters.note: The core teaching is the five-level cosmological identification of ‘happiness, wisdom, power’ across divine domains (¶5–¶8). The chapter opens with a clear hagiographic/dialogue frame (¶1–¶4). A strong editorial seam occurs when the patterned formula is extended to the institutional church (¶9), followed by a brief exhortatory/pastoral closure (¶10), consistent with the chapter’s pastoral drift signal.

chapters.title: Concerning the Four Great Days that have come forth from one another, together with the Four Nights
chapters.note: The chapter is predominantly systematic cosmological enumeration (four days/four nights; twelve hours/shadows) and reads largely as an older correspondential taxonomy. The main later intrusions are (a) hagiographic/compilational framing and beatitude-style closings (¶1, ¶6, ¶17), and (b) application that maps a cosmic register onto contemporary religious institutions (“church”, “sects”) inside otherwise cosmological sentences (¶5, ¶14–¶15), producing MIXED paragraphs.

chapters.title: Concerning Four Hunters of Light and Four of Darkness.
chapters.note: This kephalaion is predominantly systematic cosmological-correspondential teaching: a fourfold “hunter / ship / sea / net” mapping for Light powers and a parallel fourfold mapping for Darkness powers. The main later layers are (a) a dialogue/frame apparatus (¶1, ¶7) and (b) beatitude-style exhortations (¶6, ¶12) plus a polemical/institutional application that identifies the Darkness-hunter with what “rules in every sect” (¶11). ¶4 largely preserves the same cosmic mapping style but includes an institutional identification (“holy church”) that appears to be a later application graft within an otherwise older correspondential unit.

chapters.title: Concerning the Five Storehouses that have poured forth from the Land of Darkness since the [Beginning]; the Five Rulers, the Five Spirits, the Five Bodies, the Five Tastes.
chapters.note: Core material dominates: a highly schematic pentadic cosmology of the Land of Darkness (storehouses → elements → trees → genera; and five worlds with kings/spirits/bodies/tastes), plus a detailed physiognomy and faculties of the King of Darkness. A strong editorial/application drift appears in the second half: several paragraphs keep the old correspondential mapping (face/metal/taste) but pivot to identifying the ‘spirit’ in contemporary institutions (principalities, leaders, temples, sects, soothsayers) and to direct exhortation.

chapters.title: The Seventh, concerning the Five Fathers
chapters.note: The opening half is a tightly ordered cosmological emanation/evocation schema (Father of Greatness → three emanations; Third Ambassador → three powers; Jesus the Splendour → three powers), in an impersonal expository voice typical of the older substrate. The second half shows strong editorial fatigue: the schema is redirected toward institutional identifications (apostles/churches/elect/catechumens) and includes a Johannine-style saying (Jn 8 vector), plus a closing beatitude/exhortation.

chapters.title: Concerning the Fourteen Vehicles that Jesus has boarded.
chapters.note: The chapter’s core is a systematic cosmological listing of ten “vehicles/carriages” (¶2–8) in which Jesus the Son of Greatness journeys through the cosmic orders. A clear editorial seam then extends the pattern to the institutional church (¶9). The closing paragraph (¶10) begins as a structural arithmetic summary (likely closing the older list) but then shifts into later soteriological/praise material (beatitude-style blessing and polemical antithesis). Strong editorial fatigue signal aligns with the late ecclesial extension and closing exhortative tone.

chapters.title: The Explanation of the Peace, what it is; the Right Hand; the Kiss; the Salutation.
chapters.note: The chapter opens with a clear dialogue-question frame, then presents a largely self-contained cosmological archetype: five “signs/mysteries” enacted in the descent/ascent of the First Man (peace, right hand, kiss, salutation, laying on of hands). Mid-chapter the editor repeatedly pivots from archetype to human social ritual (“in the midst of mankind”, “here and now”, “today”), producing multiple MIXED paragraphs. The second half shows strong editorial fatigue: institutional church initiation sequence, exhortation, and clerical authority material dominate. One paragraph contains a likely biblical/psalmic quotation about sitting at the right hand/footstool, treated as OVERLAY inside an otherwise cosmological unit (handled as MIXED with the citation removed).

chapters.title: Concerning the Interpretation of the Fourteen [Great Aeons] of Light, about which Sethel has spoken in [his Prayer]
chapters.note: Core teaching dominates from ¶3–¶5: a systematic fourteenfold cosmological enumeration (5+2+5+2) and its function in sustaining/establishing the universe. ¶1–¶2 are compilation frame (disciples’ question + dialogue attribution). ¶5 is more expansive and lacunose, but it remains within the cosmic system (Ambassador’s kingship among aeons) rather than pivoting to contemporary institutions or exhortation.

chapters.title: [Concerning the Interpretation of] all [the] Fathers of [Light], who are distinguished from one another.
chapters.note: This chapter is a catechetical-style catalogue of principal Light divinities. Most paragraphs are written in a repetitive “The beginning of X is Y” application register that maps cosmic beings onto worldly virtues/roles (grace, prayer, hunters, builders, etc.), suggesting a later didactic recasting of an older list. The recoverable core is the underlying enumeration of named Fathers of Light and a few brief cosmological functions (notably the Living Spirit and his five sons; the Light Mind as awakener/gatherer). The opening speech-attribution is frame, and the closing beatitudes are exhortational/pastoral.

chapters.title: Concerning the Interpretation of the Five Words that are proclaimed in the Universe
chapters.note: The chapter is extremely fragmentary. Paragraph 1 is a clear hagiographic Q&A frame anchored in contemporary sectarian labels (Baptists, ‘Purified Ones’), while ¶2–¶3 preserve brief internal identifications of the “words” with Manichaean cosmological divinities (Father; Third Ambassador). The identifications themselves stay cosmos→cosmos, but the overall setup likely reflects a later syncretic/interpretive agenda (Mandaean/Elchasaite parallels flagged in the apparatus).

chapters.title: Concerning the Five Saviours, the Resurrectors of Those Who Are Dead, Together with the Five Resurrections
chapters.note: This kephalaion is structurally pentadic (enumerating resurrectors) with a clear hagiographic opening frame and a likely late concluding beatitude. The central numbered sequence (¶3–¶6) is impersonal, cosmological, and process-oriented, consistent with the older teaching substrate, though heavily lacunose.

chapters.title: The Interpretation [of] the S[i]lence, the Fast, [the Peace], the Day, [and] the Rest; [what] they are.
chapters.note: This chapter is largely an interpretive apparatus mapping named church “lessons” (silence/fast/peace/day/rest) onto cosmological archetypes. That mapping move (ritual term → cosmic entity) is later than the oldest substrate, but several paragraphs preserve clear cosmological fragments (First Man, ship of living waters, great aeon, Pillar of Glory). Frame material appears at the opening (disciples’ request) and in a brief doxological close.

chapters.title: [Concerning the ... ...] Five [Parts ...] Worlds of [...]
chapters.note: Dominant old teaching layer: a systematic pentadic/decadic cosmology of Death’s five elements and five worlds, doubling into male/female to yield twelve parts, then correlated with zodiacal signs. Late hagiographic frame appears in ¶1 and a doxological close in ¶10. The main editorial graft is ¶8–¶9, where the cosmic scheme is explicitly applied to the “holy church” and contemporary “sects,” i.e., cosmos → present institution/polemic.

chapters.title: [Concerning the Five] Greatnesses who [went forth] against the Darkness.
chapters.note: The chapter is largely a systematic cosmological pentad teaching (five greatnesses and their series) followed by process/simile expositions of the “advents” of key Light powers (First Man, Living Spirit, Third Ambassador, summons/obedience). A thin hagiographic opening formula is present (¶1). A distinct Christian/parabolic overlay appears in the Jesus the Splendour “trees/fig-garden” section and its move into Adam/Eve and “good news” language (¶23–25). The closing beatitude/exhortation (¶30) reads as later pastoral framing, consistent with mild end-of-chapter editorial drift.

chapters.title: The Chapter of the Three Seasons
chapters.note: This kephalaion is dominated by systematic cosmological time-structuring (three seasons: descent/ascent of the First Man; ordering of the universe; final redemptive span from the Ambassador’s Image to the ascent of the Statue). The only clear later material is the dialogue frame apparatus ("apostle", "disciples" Q&A attributions), which wraps or punctuates otherwise core teaching. No NT citation formulae or institutional/pastoral grafts appear; “Jesus” here reads as the mythic/cosmic saviour-agent within the Manichaean system rather than a Gospel overlay.

chapters.title: Concerning the Five War[s that the] Sons of [Li]ght waged with the Sons] of Darkness.
chapters.note: Most of the chapter preserves a systematic cosmological sequence (five wars: First Man, Living Spirit, Third Ambassador, Jesus the glorious one, counsel of life). Two clear later intrusions occur: (a) a dialogue attribution framing the opening line (FRAME), and (b) a Gospel/"saviour" citation in the First Man section (NT entry-vector). The final lines shift toward ecclesial beatitude language ("elect") and generic moral victory formulae, consistent with the detected late pastoral drift.

chapters.title: Concerning the Five Releases: what they are
chapters.note: This chapter is largely a systematic five-fold cosmological enumeration of “releases/savings” (First Man → Living Spirit → Third Ambassador → Jesus the Splendour → Great Counsel/Summons-and-Obedience), a classic substrate pattern. A brief hagiographic dialogue tag opens the chapter (¶1), and there are later expansions where the mapping crosses from cosmic mechanics into institutional/Christian-historical reference (notably “churches” and “flesh” in ¶6, and “apostles/commandment” in ¶12). The closing beatitude/exhortation (¶13) reads as later pastoral/application voice rather than impersonal exposition.

chapters.title: The Chapter of the Name of the Fathers
chapters.note: Chapter is dominated by systematic cosmological title→realm (“greatness”) correspondences for multiple divine figures. The only clear later material is the dialogue frame in ¶1–2 and the attribution tag in ¶3; no pastoral drift or NT citation overlay is present.

chapters.title: [C]oncerning the Father of Gr[eat]ness: [ho]w he is established and determined.
chapters.note: After a brief hagiographic/dialogue incipit (¶1), the chapter is almost entirely a systematic, impersonal cosmological exposition: the Father of Greatness established in five light limbs (storehouses/qualities) and also in twelve light limbs (wisdoms), then a sequential description of the five. No explicit institutional, exhortational, or NT-overlay material appears in the preserved text; the low teaching-density in ¶8 seems driven by damage/lacunae rather than a register shift.

chapters.title: [On] the Land of Light
chapters.note: This kephalaion is almost entirely cosmological description (land of Light, its beings and features) with a strong five-fold/aeonic correspondential register. There is no clear institutional/pastoral drift; the only likely late/editorial material is the rubric-like heading and a closing beatitude-style line.

chapters.title: [ ... ] which [ ... ]
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly cosmological-cosmogonic narrative in an impersonal, system-internal register (Darkness/Death stirring, five dark elements, storehouses/abyss, ruler’s counsel, Father of Greatness, First Man and the five garments/sons). No NT citation formulas or church-institutional/pastoral material appear. The only clear later material is minor discourse framing (address) and a meta-teaching comment about who is permitted/able to “teach about it,” including the term “apostle[s].”

Despite the synopsis’s ‘composite’ character, most paragraphs preserve an older cosmological time-measure teaching: emanation durations are expressed by internal cosmic imagery (storehouses, aeons, borders, descent/ascent, Last Statue, chaining). A later editorial/meta-teaching layer appears where the text pivots to what ‘apostles/teachers/chosen’ can or cannot proclaim about the two eternities; these paragraphs are treated as non-core. Several paragraphs are MIXED where brief audience-address or transmission talk (‘listen’, ‘I recounted to you’, ‘disciples’) introduces otherwise core cosmological exposition.

chapters.title: [Concerning the Advent of Five Fathers from the Five Limbs of the Father]
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by a compact five-fold correspondential mapping: five divine/cosmic hypostases are said to “come from” five internal faculties/limbs of the Father (mind, thought, insight, counsel, consideration). ¶1 is a later dialogue/frame header (“the apostle speaks”); ¶2–¶3 read as impersonal, systematic cosmological exposition with no institutional or Gospel anchoring.

chapters.title: Concerning the First Man and the Ambassador and the Ship; what they resemble.
chapters.note: This chapter is largely a set of internally-cosmological similes (First Man, Living Spirit, Great Spirit in the Ship, Ambassador) describing redemption within the Manichaean system. Only the final paragraph pivots into direct exhortation to disciples (application voice), marking a later pastoral graft. Paragraph 1 contains a clear hagiographic/frame attribution that must be stripped to recover the teaching.

chapters.title: Concerning the Five Forms that exist in the Rulers of Darkness.
chapters.note: The chapter is dominated by a systematic correspondential body→world mapping (five forms from the five worlds of darkness) followed by additional triads of ruler-qualities. The final two paragraphs pivot into direct second-person exhortation (“my beloved ones…”)—an application/pastoral add-on consistent with the chapter’s strong second-half drift signal. The opening contains a hagiographic seating/speaking frame that must be stripped to recover the core teaching introduction.

chapters.title: [Concerning the T]welve Judges [of] the Father
chapters.note: This chapter is largely a systematic cosmological catalogue of twelve judging powers emanated from the Father of Greatness (CORE). The opening dialogue tag is a late hagiographic frame (¶1), and the closing exhortation to the community is pastoral/application (¶16), consistent with the chapter’s strong second-half drift. Two list-items show later institutional/Manichaean-church coloring inside an otherwise cosmic sequence: (a) Jesus the Splendour labelled “father of all the apostles” (¶10), and (b) Light Mind “choos[ing] the holy church” (¶13); these are best treated as MIXED with the ecclesial identifiers removed.

chapters.title: Concerning the Eighteen Great Thrones of all the Fathers
chapters.note: This chapter is largely a systematic, numbered cosmological catalogue (thrones across aeons/ships/firmaments), characteristic of the older teaching layer. A later compiler has wrapped it with a dialogue opening (¶1) and appended/extended the sequence with ecclesial-apostolic identification (¶17) and summary/doxological material (¶11–12, ¶18). One paragraph (¶10) shows a pivot from cosmic identification to institutional reference (“churches”), suggesting editorial application grafted onto a core throne-item.

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Garments
chapters.note: This is a short, largely continuous cosmological instruction about the Living Spirit’s three ‘garments’ (wind, fire, water) and their spatial deployment across the zone. The only clear later material is the formulaic dialogue opening and direct address in ¶1; otherwise the chapter stays within cosmos→cosmos description without institutional or NT overlay.

chapters.title: Concerning the Summons, in which Limb of the Soul it descended to the First Man.
chapters.note: The chapter is overwhelmingly cosmological-correspondential teaching about the First Man as Head and the scattered Living Soul as limbs, with systematic body↔cosmos analogy and a fivefold faculty list. It is embedded in a late Q&A dialogue frame (teachers/enlightener) and contains one citation-like appeal to “scriptures” in the question, but no clear NT/Gospel entry vector. The second-half “drift” here reads more as narrative elaboration than institutional/pastoral graft.

chapters.title: Concerning the Seven Works of the Living Spirit
chapters.note: The chapter is dominated by a compact, enumerated cosmological teaching: the Living Spirit’s “seven works” (plus an added eschatological work) described in impersonal mythic/architectonic terms (rescuing First Man, constructing zone/ships, appointing powers, etc.). Only the opening dialogue attribution (“Once again the enlightener speaks”) and the final beatitude read as later framing/devotional material rather than the older systematic substrate.

chapters.title: Concerning the Five Things that he constructed with the hard Bodies of the Rulers
chapters.note: A short, systematic five-item construction list attributed to the Living Spirit. The only clear later layer is the formulaic dialogue/frame attribution in the opening clause of ¶1; the rest reads as impersonal cosmological-architectural instruction within the mythic system (no institutional application, exhortation, or NT overlay).

chapters.title: Concerning the Ten Things that the Ambassador began by his Advent
chapters.note: A compact numbered schematic of ten cosmological operations triggered by the Third Ambassador’s advent. Aside from the single dialogue attribution in ¶1 (hagiographic frame), the chapter stays entirely within the cosmic system (ships, wheels, doors, separation of Night/Day, Sin, abortions, transmigrations) and reads like an old structural list rather than institutional application or NT overlay.

chapters.title: Concerning the Four Works of the Ambassador
chapters.note: This chapter is essentially a compact, systematic fourfold exposition (image; doors of firmaments; purification/release of light; manifestation of the light ship and living soul). The only clearly later material is the brief dialogue/frame attribution in ¶1 (“Once again the enlightener speaks:”), which wraps an otherwise core, impersonal cosmological statement.

chapters.title: Concerning the Wheel that exists in front of the King of Honour
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly systematic cosmological exposition about the Wheel before the King of Honour in the seventh firmament, functioning as a binding/diagnostic device over the rulers and powers. Only the opening dialogue attribution (“apostle speaks”) is a later framing tag; the rest maintains an impersonal, structural voice and stays within the cosmic architecture (firmaments, rulers, zone, fetter, seals, shining men). Paragraph 5’s simile (chain/guard) is a generic illustrative comparison and does not clearly anchor to institutional or NT material, though it may be a secondary explanatory gloss.

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Zones.
chapters.note: Apart from a brief formulaic incipit, the chapter is compact, systematic cosmological exposition: a three-zone architecture built from nested fivefold sets (Powers of Darkness → sons of the Man → sons of the [Living] Spirit), described as a suspension/structural-dependence mechanism within the cosmic edifice. No NT citation, exhortation, or institutional application appears.

chapters.title: Concerning the Light Mind and the Apostles and the Saints
chapters.note: Core substrate dominates the middle of the chapter: systematic macrocosm↔microcosm mapping (universe-as-human; five intellectuals; watch-district rebellions; Light Mind’s binding/releasing operations; new man formation). The opening and closing are a dialogue/hagiographic frame, and the second half shows strong pastoral drift: institutional repair scenes (teachers/presbyters/brethren), exhortational watch-language, and a long self-praise/apostolate section. Several paragraphs are MIXED where a cosmological mechanism pivots into contemporary-institutional polemic (church/apostles, idol-worship catalogues).

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Days and the Two Deaths
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly a systematic eschatological/cosmological teaching (three ‘days’ as three great temporal-cosmic phases; two ‘deaths’ as two distinct modes of loss/separation). The only clear frame is the opening dialogue apparatus. A late Christianising moral-causal tag appears at the end of ¶15 (‘blasphemed … the Holy Spirit’), appended to an otherwise cosmological description of the second death.

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Things that were established by the Light
chapters.note: Aside from a short formulaic opening frame, the chapter is a tightly structured, impersonal triadic exposition of eschatological cosmology: three necessary constructions by the Light (new earth; coffin/prison for the Enemy; fate of the condemned) culminating in the mechanics of eternal separation/sterilisation. Despite one paragraph using moral vocabulary (“sinners”, “wicked deeds”), it functions as doctrinal mechanism within the cosmic system rather than institutional exhortation.

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Blows that befell the Enemy because of the Light.
chapters.note: Nearly the whole chapter is impersonal, system-description eschatology: three sequential ‘blows’/wars and the final binding/separation of Darkness. Only the opening dialogue-attribution (‘Once again he turned, and says:’) is a later compilation frame; no NT citation and no institutional/pastoral application occurs.

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Vessels
chapters.note: The chapter is largely dominated by a systematic cosmological teaching about how the Living Spirit uses three “garments” (wind/water/fire) to discharge and then confine three dark “vessels” (water/darkness/fire), expressed through extended medical and birth analogies and a timed process. The second-half ‘twelve deeds’ enumeration is mostly cosmological, but shows editorial fatigue: explicit institutional/present-world anchoring appears (notably the fasting line; and an ‘apostles’ paragraph), and several paragraphs retain dialogue-attribution seams.

chapters.title: Concerning the Vessels.
chapters.note: The chapter is dominated by systematic cosmological process-description (discharge/sweeping of the three dark vessels; purification of firmaments and earths; remnant signs in the created order). The dialogue attributions (“disciples…”, “apostle…”, “enlightener…”) function as later compilation frame; once stripped, the remaining teaching stays inside the cosmic system (cosmos→cosmos mapping) with no institutional or NT overlay.

chapters.title: Concerning the Sea Giant
chapters.note: Aside from the formulaic opening, the chapter reads as continuous cosmological mechanism: the purification-washing of vessels/wheels, the deposition of residues into the sea, and the technical function of the Sea Giant as astral fetter and mixing-vessel. No explicit institutional application, hagiographic Q&A, or NT citation intrudes; even the coin-moulding analogy functions as internal correspondential explanation of how many astral "impressions" become one monstrous body.

chapters.title: Concerning the Vessels
chapters.note: This chapter is almost entirely systematic cosmological logistics: foreprepared containment-places for hostile beings and wastes, expressed in impersonal, process-oriented voice (“Before X…, a place was constructed…”). No dialogue frame, no Gospel/NT citation, and no institutional/pastoral application. A few motifs (watchers/giants) may reflect later syncretic mythic material within Manichaean cosmology, but the diction remains within the cosmic system rather than pointing to contemporary institutions.

chapters.title: Concerning the Ambassador.
chapters.note: The chapter is largely an old, impersonal cosmological sequence of foreordination (“before …”) describing predetermined moments in the Light’s plan: Ambassador, ships, Judge, astrological fate, destroyers, and the Builder. It is lightly framed by an introductory exhortation (¶1). One paragraph (¶5) crosses from cosmic architecture into contemporaneous polemic (“sects”), indicating an editorial/institutional application graft rather than substrate teaching.

chapters.title: Concerning the Four great Things
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly the systematic cosmological layer: a fourfold division of the ruling-power across cosmic structures (ten firmaments, eight earths, walls/vessels, and the wheel/sphere of the stars), including a mechanical rationale for binding and balancing hostile powers. Only the opening dialogue attribution is hagiographic frame; no NT citation or institutional/pastoral extension appears.

chapters.title: Concerning the Conduits.
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly a continuous cosmological-mechanical teaching about three cosmic conduits/roots binding heavenly structures to earthly bodies, governing ascent of Life and descent of waste, and explaining astral ‘authority’ via the Ambassador episode. Later material is limited to dialogue/frame attributions ("Once again…", "the apostle says", disciple entreaties), which are stripped where present. Despite a mild second-half drift signal, there is no clear institutional/church graft; the late layer is mainly hagiographic Q&A packaging.

chapters.title: Concerning the Wheel and the Conduits
chapters.note: The chapter is predominantly a compact piece of cosmological-mechanical teaching: why the celestial wheel does not shear or snag the conduits. Only the opening disciple-question is hagiographic frame; the remainder is core explanation using correspondential analogies (ship through water; bird through air).

chapters.title: Concerning these Names: God, Rich One, and Angel; who they are.
chapters.note: The chapter is largely systematic, cosmological definition: a threefold taxonomy (god/rich one/angel) repeated across three moments (archetypes in the Land of Light; emanations engaged in the cosmic contest; households of major Light-beings). The opening Q&A is a later hagiographic frame. One paragraph (¶9) pivots from internal cosmological genealogy into mission-language (“apostolate… hope and confidence”), suggesting a later rhetorical/application expansion within an otherwise core sequence.

chapters.title: Concerning the First Man.
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly a compact cosmological-mechanical exposition of the First Man’s descent and the five garments (living fire plus four helpers), explaining wounding, mixture, and the exceptional status of air. The only clear late layer is the brief hagiographic speech-introduction in ¶1. Despite the chapter-level ‘fatigue’ warning, the surviving second-half paragraphs here remain within cosmos→cosmos description (no institutional or NT overlay).

chapters.title: Concerning the [ ... ] of the Light
chapters.note: This chapter is largely an exhortative homily on unity, using Light/Darkness as exempla and then directly addressing the community. Only small fragments preserve an older cosmological claim (unity/order in the Light; division in the Darkness). The extended comparison to "the kingdom of this world" and the second-person imperatives mark later application/pastoral expansion.

chapters.title: Concerning the First Man.
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly core cosmological teaching: First Man’s descent, the hunting/snaring of Matter and the rulers, and the devastation of the storehouses, illustrated through correspondential analogies (marsh/net; body/head/limbs). Only the opening dialogue attribution in ¶1 is later frame.

chapters.title: [Concerning] the Quality of the Garments
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly cosmological-architectural teaching (Living Spirit / Father of Life building and ordering the cosmos from the mixture), expressed through sustained correspondential metaphors (architect/carpenter) that remain inside the cosmic system. Only ¶1 contains an explicit dialogue-attribution frame formula; no NT citations or institutional/pastoral grafts appear despite the chapter-level fatigue warning.

chapters.title: Concerning the Fashioning of Adam
chapters.note: This chapter is largely cosmological teaching about the Third Ambassador’s displayed Image and the rulers’ imitation that results in Adam and Eve, plus a short doctrinal appendix on other non-sexually-generated figures (sea-giant, sea-monster, vegetation). The main later material is (a) the dialogue/Q&A frame (¶1–2) and (b) the extended worldly parable of the ‘free woman’ (¶5–6) and brief exhortative closure (¶8). No NT citation vectors appear; the key discriminator is cosmos→cosmos exposition versus cosmos→worldly illustration.

chapters.title: [Concerning Saklas and his Powers]
chapters.note: The chapter preserves a large block of systematic microcosm teaching (senses as “storehouses,” gates/orifices with guards, Light Mind taking the bolts), which reads like an older correspondential substrate. It is wrapped in Kephalaia dialogue attributions (“the enlightener speaks/says”) and ends with clear late application/exhortation. A key substrate→application boundary occurs where the mechanism of sense-control is illustrated with contemporary luxury/temptation imagery (kings’ garments, silken women) and then with explicitly communal/devotional items (psalms, prayers, hymns).

chapters.title: Concerning the Generation of Adam.
chapters.note: The oldest layer here is a compact astrological-cosmological explanation: five time-authorities (year/month/day/hour/moment) installed over the zodiac-sphere, whose changing dominion correlates with the diminishing lifespan/stature of human generations, plus an older-looking biological consequence of “richer light” in the earliest generations (multiple births). The chapter is strongly wrapped in dialogue frame, and the second half shows marked homiletic/application drift (end-times emphasis; moralizing about present humanity), consistent with editorial fatigue.

chapters.title: The Four Powers that grieve
chapters.note: The chapter opens with a hagiographic speech frame and closes with institutional/eschatological application (notably pastoral drift in ¶4–5). The oldest layer is concentrated in ¶2–3: impersonal cosmological description of the Mother of Life and the First Man grieving for their children/sons amid the Darkness, ruling-power, and enemy assault. ¶4 shifts to Mani’s church-mission register (holy church, persecution, Light Mind) and ¶5 to Christian eschatological vocabulary (gehenna, repentance).

chapters.title: The Chapter of the Elements that wept
chapters.note: The chapter is dominated by a systematic fourfold teaching sequence about the garments/elements and their staged weeping within the cosmological drama (First Man, Living Spirit, Last Statue). A clear late drift appears at the end: the discourse pivots from cosmic description to justificatory/hagiographic talk about “apostles…prophets” suffering to save souls, followed by an admonitory maxim—consistent with the strong editorial-fatigue signal.

chapters.title: [Concerning the Four Fathers; what they are like.]
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly core correspondential teaching: a systematic body→cosmos mapping (hidden/visible organs ↔ hidden/visible divine realities; eyes ↔ light-ships; tongue ↔ Jesus the Splendour). The only clear late layer is the dialogue attribution in ¶1 (frame) and the concluding summarizing flourish in ¶9 (frame-style closure). No NT citation formulae or institutional/pastoral grafts appear.

chapters.title: Concerning the Garment of the Waters: how great is its Measure.
chapters.note: This chapter is wrapped in a strong hagiographic-historical frame (Shapur, Tigris flood, disciples’ praise). The oldest layer appears mainly in the middle as systematic cosmological explanation of the First Man’s elemental garments and the ‘garment of waters’ being drunk by the rulers of death, with sevenfold/measure language. Several teaching units are embedded in dialogue attributions and occasional first-person/citational phrases (e.g., reference to the ‘Great Gospel’), which look like later compilation-layer delivery rather than the impersonal substrate.

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Rocks
chapters.note: This chapter is largely core cosmological teaching (three stabilizing "rocks" set within the worlds), with a brief hagiographic opening (¶1) and a late institutional/application graft in ¶5 that relocates the third rock into "the holy church" (consistent with the strong editorial fatigue signal in the second half).

chapters.title: Concerning Love.
chapters.note: The chapter preserves a short cosmological definition of Love (as the Father of Greatness) and Hate (as Death/Darkness mechanics), with a later ecclesial-Christian expansion: paragraph 3 pivots to the holy church, the apostle, and an explicit Gospel-style citation (Jn 15:13 / Jn 1 noted in apparatus), indicating later overlay. The opening of ¶1 and the attribution in ¶4 are hagiographic frame wrapping otherwise older teaching.

chapters.title: [Concerning Adam]
chapters.note: After a brief hagiographic opening, the chapter is dominated by systematic, enumerated cosmological exposition (three preeminences in Adam; seven intentions of the rulers). The mappings remain within the Manichaean cosmic system (image of the Ambassador, five sons, elements, zodiac/time-powers) with no NT citation formulas or institutional/pastoral applications, so the teaching body reads as core substrate material.

chapters.title: Concerning the Sun.
chapters.note: The oldest layer here is largely a numbered, systematic correspondential teaching: (a) seven benefits of the Sun vs. seven evils of Night, (b) five archetypes in the Sun, and (c) three further Sun-qualities corresponding to the Father of Greatness. Later hands add (i) a hagiographic dialogue setting (“the apostle… among his disciples”), (ii) polemic/application against “sects,” (iii) a scriptural/legal anti-Jewish passage about a “law” forbidding worship of the sun, and (iv) explicit Gospel/NT overlay at the close (Thomas saying; “children of light/day” language) plus concluding blessings/exhortation (editorial fatigue in the second half).

chapters.title: Concerning the Ambassador.
chapters.note: The chapter contains a substantial correspondential-cosmological exposition (sunrise/sunset as revelations of the First Man’s descent and the Last Statue’s ascent). The opening and closing are hagiographic frame. A strong late drift occurs near the end: an explicit exhortation to preach/repentance (pastoral/application layer) follows a self-contained cosmological teaching sequence, consistent with the editorial-fatigue signal.

chapters.title: Concerning the Light-Giver.
chapters.note: This chapter reads as a homiletic analogy (sun → Mani and the elect) embedded in a formulaic discourse frame. It is dominated by application voice (imperatives, first-person self-reference) and institutional terms (disciples, congregation, elect, charity). No systematic cosmos→cosmos correspondential mapping appears; the analogy is used to point to Mani and communal ethics rather than to expound an impersonal cosmological mechanism.

chapters.title: Concerning Fire.
chapters.note: A compact five-fold classification of the works of visible fire. Apart from a brief dialogue-attribution incipit, the chapter is continuous systematic teaching: numbered structure, impersonal explanatory voice, and correspondential registers (separation into components; taste/aroma/heat/light) without ecclesial or NT overlay.

chapters.title: Concerning the Twelve Signs of the Zodiac and the Five Stars
chapters.note: The chapter is dominated by systematic cosmological-astral teaching: a pentadic derivation of zodiac/planets from the five worlds of Darkness, a four-sided distribution on the sphere, and correspondential effects on creatures. The main later layer is the dialogue/question frame (¶1) and several first-person recap/closure units (¶10–12). A few paragraphs contain compilational discourse markers (“I reveal…”) that can be stripped while preserving a coherent impersonal teaching substrate (¶2, ¶8, ¶13).

chapters.title: Concerning the Body: It was constructed after the Pattern of the Universe.
chapters.note: The dominant layer is CORE: systematic microcosm–macrocosm correspondences (body parts ↔ cosmic zones, five watch-stations, four bodily ‘worlds’ with sevens, and zodiac-to-body schemas). A later PASTORAL graft (¶17–24) reuses the cosmological pattern to interpret ethical self-mastery and the ‘elect’ life; this crosses from cosmos→cosmos mapping into cosmos→community/behavior application. The chapter is wrapped and re-started by small FRAME dialogue-attribution formulas (¶1, ¶30, ¶37). No NT/explicit Gospel overlay appears.

chapters.title: Concerning the Gathering in of the [E]lements.
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly a compact, systematic cosmological sequence: a chain of gathering/translation from element to element and then through the salvific cosmic stations (Answer → Summons → purified Mind → Pillar → First Man → Ambassador → aeons). The only clear later layer is the dialogue attribution in ¶1, which functions as a hagiographic framing seam over an otherwise substantive question.

chapters.title: Concerning the worn and torn apart Garments, or the tattered Clothes, or the Elements, the Cross, and the rest too.
chapters.note: After a short dialogue frame (¶1–6) the chapter consists of systematic definitional cosmology (¶7–15): a series of internal mappings that equate named “garment” terms with specific light-powers and their stations/functions in the cosmic architecture. No clear institution-pointing seam occurs; the second half remains within cosmos→cosmos exposition despite the chapter-level fatigue warning.

chapters.title: Concerning the Envy of Matter
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by later editorial/application material (notably in the second half: Mani-self reference, church/catechumen categories, exhortation). The oldest recoverable layer is a short cosmological-mythic sequence defining Envy as native to the worlds of darkness and narrating Matter’s envy against key cosmic/human figures (First Man; the Ambassador’s image; Adam). The opening contains a dialogue-frame attribution that must be stripped.

chapters.title: Concerning the living Fire: It is present in Eight Places.
chapters.note: This chapter is almost entirely systematic cosmological teaching: an eightfold ‘places wherein it is’ enumeration locating the living fire across Light-land, Father, First Man/Perfect Man, the two light ships, Living Spirit’s body, and the new earth. The only clear later material is the dialogue/frame attribution ‘Once again the apostle speaks’ in ¶1; otherwise the voice stays impersonal and intra-cosmic, with no institutional application and no NT overlay.

chapters.title: [Concerning the Letter (?)]
chapters.note: The chapter opens with a brief hagiographic frame, then preserves a compact core teaching (¶2–3) describing the primordial summons and answer between the Living Spirit and the First Man as divinised “letters” containing total foreknowledge of events. From ¶4 onward the pattern is extended to the holy church, good works, and direct exhortation—consistent with the strong editorial-fatigue signal and institutional/application drift.

chapters.title: [Conce]rning Lord Manichaios: how he journeyed.
chapters.note: This chapter is almost entirely hagiographic-biographical narrative (Mani’s journeys, summons by Shapur, opposition by rulers/sects) framed as dialogue, with a late Christian overlay via the Johannine dictum about the world loving darkness. The second half drifts into explicit exhortation/prayer for the community (holy church), but there is no recoverable systematic cosmos→cosmos correspondential teaching substrate here.

chapters.title: The Chapter of the Four Kingdoms
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly a late homiletic/pastoral piece built around a Gospel saying (bread and water to a disciple) and applied to Manichaean community categories (catechumens, righteous/elect), with exhortation to almsgiving and promise of eschatological reward. It lacks the hallmark “cosmos→cosmos” systematic correspondential mappings (degrees, body–universe maps, cosmic mechanics). The opening is explicitly hagiographic frame (“the apostle speaks”), and the rest is an ethical application contrasting charity with the worldly “four kingdoms.”

chapters.title: Concerning the Four Things over which People kill each other.
chapters.note: This chapter reads as a homiletic/moral catalogue of “worldly” pursuits (food, sex, wealth, war/glory) followed by direct exhortation (“I say to you… accept faith…”) and a brief mortality conclusion. It lacks the substrate’s hallmark cosmos→cosmos correspondential mapping (degree-structures, realm↔metal/taste/form correspondences, systematic cosmography). The light/dark language appears only as soteriological application within a second-person address, consistent with later pastoral/application material; no extractable core block is present.

chapters.title: Concerning the Fasting of the Saints
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by late institutional/pastoral material (fasting practice, saints, weekly observance, alms), with a small embedded cosmological-mechanistic substrate about (a) the soul/light entering via food and (b) the purity-state of the Children of Light. The strong editorial-fatigue signal fits the drift into explicit communal regulation in the final paragraphs.

chapters.title: The Chapter of the Commandments of Righteousness
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly institutional/disciplinary (elect vs. catechumens, fasting/prayer/alms, sexual and dietary restrictions). Even where cosmological terms appear (Cross of Light; sun and moon as light-givers), they function as ethical/institutional applications rather than cosmos→cosmos mapping. It opens with a hagiographic dialogue attribution, and the latter paragraphs show clear editorial/institutional expansion (consistent with the strong chapter-level editorial-fatigue signal and the seam flag in ¶7).

chapters.title: The Chapter of Fasting, for it engenders a Host of Angels
chapters.note: This kephalaion is dominated by hagiographic dialogue frame and institutional/pastoral material (elect/catechumens, lord’s day fasts, church leadership, building churches, alms, exemption from office). The key doctrinal claim—‘seven angels’ engendered by fasting—is presented only as a church-practice rule and is immediately embedded in congregational narrative and exhortation, not in a self-contained cosmic mapping/mechanics exposition. No recoverable pre-compilation correspondential substrate is present in a form separable from the later ecclesial setting.

chapters.title: The Chapter of Righteous [Judgement]
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by later dialogical/pastoral material about anger, reprimand, repentance, and conduct among ‘brothers/sisters’, wrapped in Kephalaia-style Q&A frame. A single brief cosmological-correspondential fragment (¶9) grounds the ethical ‘two aspects’ (love/fear) in the heavenly light-givers’ purificatory function; it stays entirely within the cosmic system and reads like an older teaching insert. An NT paraphrase (Mt 6:21) appears in ¶10, marking Christian overlay there.

chapters.title: Concerning the Man who is ugly in his Body, [but] beautiful [in his Soul].
chapters.note: The chapter opens with a hagiographic congregation scene and a moralizing address that culminates in a Gospel-derived saying (overlay). The oldest recoverable substrate concentrates in the impersonal, process-style teaching on pearl formation (¶9–13) and the cosmological return/rest of freed souls in the aeons (¶17). The explicit identification of the image with “the holy church” and “apostles” is an editorial application graft (¶15–16), followed by exhortation (¶18).

chapters.title: Concerning Wisdom; it is far superior when on the Tongue than in the Heart of the Person.
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by a didactic analogy-teaching (child-in-womb/birth; fire-in-wood/light) with a dialogue wrapper. It lacks the hallmark “cosmos→cosmos” systematic architecture (named aeons, degree-lists, body/universe maps), so the extracted ‘core’ here is best understood as an older homiletic correspondential instruction embedded in a Kephalaia Q&A frame rather than a clear fragment of the deepest cosmological substrate. No NT citation overlay or institutional/pastoral graft is present; the primary late layer is the hagiographic dialogue frame (apostle/disciple, rejoicing/obeisance closure).

chapters.title: Concerning the Cross of Light: [...] trample upon it.
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by later practical/pastoral casuistry (travel, obedience to superiors, alms-collection, elect/catechumen relations) with clear editorial fatigue in the second half. The oldest recoverable layer appears mainly as a self-contained teaching unit using the doctor/healing analogy to explain why “trampling” that causes short-term distress does not incur guilt when done for healing/liberation; one NT/Gospel saying is inserted into that teaching (overlay).

chapters.title: The Chapter of the Man who asks: Why [am] I sometimes at peace, and troubled at other times?
chapters.note: The chapter is a dialogue: a heavy frame/question section (¶1–5) including experiential self-report and a clearly institutional/pious vignette (¶4), followed by a compact cosmological-mechanistic answer about the Light Mind, astrological disturbance, and the mixed character of nourishment (¶6–11). No NT-citation overlay appears; the main late material is the hagiographic/dialogue apparatus and recap-style address to the disciple.

chapters.title: Concerning the Alms, that [ ... ] life in the Church.
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by institutional/almsgiving material about the holy church and catechumens (pastoral/editorial extension). The oldest cosmological teaching appears mainly in ¶7–10, where the ascent of the living soul through the sun and moon and the resting of the light-givers in the Land of Light is described entirely within the cosmic system (no church application).

chapters.title: Concerning the Catechumen who found fault with the Elect: why he is angry.
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by dialogue frame and pastoral/institutional exhortation (catechumen vs. elect/saints). Only small embedded fragments read like older doctrinal exposition (dual-essence anthropology; the divine element from the heights; the foreignness of the body/flesh of Sin). There is no sustained systematic correspondential mapping sequence here; the ‘core’ appears only as brief doctrinal clauses pressed into a disciplinary argument.

chapters.title: The Chapter of the Nazorean who questions the Teacher
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by hagiographic dialogue frame and a moral-theological apologetic about God as judge. It contains no systematic cosmological-correspondential mapping (the diagnostic of the oldest substrate). The explicit Gospel/NT vector appears in the “saviour has said” quotation and in the term “gehenna,” marking Christian overlay. The remainder reads as later didactic/pastoral reasoning rather than the impersonal, structural teaching core.

chapters.title: Concerning the Fifteen Paths; and whether the Catechumen would have avoided causing his Wealth to go on the Three Paths to Gehenna
chapters.note: The oldest layer here is relatively compact: a systematic cosmological scheme of fifteen post-mortem “paths” in the zone, with a threefold “waste” discharge to gehennas, plus a mechanistic doctrine of “deeds/wealth” as detachable substances that can be freed from the places where they are bound and travel before/with/after the soul. Much of the chapter is a later institutional/pastoral graft focused on the catechumen/elect distinction, the apostle choosing “forms” of his church, seals of faith, and discipline (fasting/prayer/alms), consistent with the flagged redaction and the strong second-half pastoral drift; paragraph 8 is a classic editorial seam extending a cosmological scheme into church predestination language.

chapters.title: Also concerning the Catechumen; shall he be saved in a single Body?
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly later institutional/pastoral instruction about catechumens (fasting, alms, church loyalty, forgiveness of sins), wrapped in dialogue and praise formulas. Only two short passages preserve older, impersonal cosmological-soteriological mechanics (post-mortem ascent/purification and the formation of the “light image”), embedded inside catechumen/church application and (once) an NT-style treasure saying.

chapters.title: The Apostle is asked: Why when you drew every thing in the Picture (- Book), did you not draw the Purification of the Catechumens who shall be cleansed by Transmigration?
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by institutional discourse (catechumen vs. elect) framed as a dialogue about Mani’s Picture-Book. It lacks the impersonal, systematic cosmos→cosmos correspondential mappings that mark the oldest teaching substrate. The second half shows strong pastoral drift (explaining catechumenal purification as ‘middle way’), consistent with later community/institutional redaction. One paragraph uses distinctly Gospel/Christian eschatological vocabulary (e.g., ‘gehenna’), best treated as Christian overlay rather than core teaching.

chapters.title: A Catechumen asked the Apostle: When I would give an Offering to the Saints, shall I inflict a Wound on the Alms?
chapters.note: This kephalaion is dominated by an institutional problem (catechumen alms for the elect) presented in Q&A form (frame + pastoral). The most plausibly older substrate-like material is the long impersonal legal/medical analogy (retaliation before a judge versus a doctor cutting a wound to heal). The explicit application to catechumens/elect/church and exhortation language is later pastoral usage of the analogy.

chapters.title: Concerning the Purification of these Four Elements [that have been place]d in the Flesh.
chapters.note: The chapter is predominantly old, systematic correspondential teaching about the four light-elements’ mixture, purification in the body, and the resulting emissions (triadic chains). It is wrapped in a brief hagiographic opening (¶1) and ends with an institutional/application paragraph about the elect vs. sinners (¶9), which crosses from cosmic mechanism to church categories.

chapters.title: The Apostle asks his Disciples: What is Cloud?
chapters.note: After a brief hagiographic dialogue frame (¶1, ¶14, ¶18), the chapter is dominated by systematic cosmological teaching: five clouds rising from the five light elements, each with a sign (lightning, thunder, storm-wind, stillness, etc.), purification of lives, and the release/seizure of rulers by angels under the Virgin of Light, culminating in confinement in the seven outer ditches/paths in the sea outside the world. Late material here is mostly dialogue attribution and recap/expository address to disciples; the underlying mechanism remains consistently cosmos→cosmos.

chapters.title: The Three Earths that Exist, they bear Fruit.
chapters.note: The chapter begins with a brief dialogue-frame formula and then presents a compact, systematic “three earths/fields” teaching. Paragraphs 1–3 remain within cosmos→cosmos correspondences (earth/field ↔ farmers ↔ ascent mechanics). Paragraph 4 is an editorial seam that extends the pattern to the institutional “holy church” (elect/catechumens) and is therefore pastoral. Paragraph 5 is explicit exhortation/application to the audience and is pastoral.

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Creations of the Flesh: the ones that were brought forth [...]; and the ones that were begotten by the Abortions; and the ones that were formed of themselves.
chapters.note: After a brief hagiographic dialogue-introduction, the chapter is a continuous, systematic teaching sequence: a threefold classification of earthly life-forms (and their propagation) grounded in Manichaean cosmology (the Ambassador, rulers/powers, and the descent of “thought” as reproductive impulse). No institutional/pastoral or NT overlay appears.

chapters.title: What is Virginal; or, otherwise, what is Continent?
chapters.note: The chapter is built as a stepped (roughly five-level) definitional sequence: ‘virginal’ vs ‘continent’ mapped to successive cosmic/processual layers of Light (aeons → mixture → purification by the Ambassador → transmigration remainder). The opening Q&A is late hagiographic frame. The middle run (¶3–8) is the strongest core substrate: impersonal cosmological/process language about mixture, purification, ascent, and transmigration. The later paragraphs pivot into institutional/ethical application (elect imagery; sexual renunciation), which reads as pastoral/Christianized extension of the pattern.

chapters.title: Concerning Transmigration
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by the Kephalaia dialogue apparatus plus institutional/pastoral differentiation between “sinners” and “catechumens,” framed as moral-educative punishment (children vs servants). It does not preserve a clearly separable cosmos→cosmos correspondential substrate; even the scattered cosmological phrases (“throne in the light,” “great fire”) occur inside an applied, disciplinary comparison aimed at community categories.

chapters.title: Concerning the Dragon with Fourteen Heads; what it is and [...]
chapters.note: The chapter’s core is a systematic microcosmic mapping: the Fourteen Heads are identified with sense/organs (upper and lower), and the Five Dens with specific internal organs/blood—an internal correspondence (body ↔ spiritual ‘Dragon’ mechanism) with no external authorities. The chapter is wrapped in a Q&A frame (disciple ↔ apostle) and closes with a devotional/praise response. A late application/pastoral drift appears where the combat with the Dragon is tied to Manichaean status language (“elect”) and reward rhetoric.

chapters.title: [Concer]ning why, if the Person shall look down into Water, [ ... ]
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by an older correspondential/scientific teaching about reflection, inversion, birth, and shadow as signs of cosmic processes (Summons/Obedience; astral ‘fathers’; body–earth fastening). A thin dialogue frame is present, and several paragraphs show a later pedagogical address (“I reveal…”, “listen…”) grafted onto otherwise cosmological exposition—best treated as MIXED rather than institutional pastoral material. The grouping is loose, consistent with redaction/textual development noted in the apparatus.

chapters.title: Concerning the Light Mind, why it does not exercise Foreknowledge for the Saint as for the Apostle?
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by dialogue frame and community-facing, practical/disciplinary reasoning about why foreknowledge is withheld from the elect (humility, avoiding disputes, avoiding mercenary divination). Even where Manichaean terms appear (Light Mind, body, revelation), they are deployed inside an institutional Q&A about elect/apostles rather than as impersonal, systematic cosmos→cosmos exposition; no recoverable correspondential substrate is present as a distinct extractable layer.

chapters.title: Concerning the Five Wonders that the Light Mind shall display in the Elect
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by institutional/ethical material (the elect preaching, faith, love, peace for brethren, and legal excommunication in the church). Only one short paragraph (¶7) reads like an impersonal cosmological-soteriological mechanism (Light Mind acting upon the new man) without direct institutional anchoring. The ending (¶9) uses strongly NT-sounding idiom (“vessel”, “pearl without price”), suggesting Christian overlay or late devotional diction.

chapters.title: Concerning Food: It shall be allocated to Five Products of the human Body.
chapters.note: After a brief hagiographic opening formula, the chapter is a compact five-fold, impersonal teaching on how sustenance is distributed into five bodily ‘productions’. There are no Gospel citations, no institutional application, and no exhortation; the discourse stays within a systematic degree-structure (food → five products), consistent with the oldest teaching style despite the non-cosmological subject matter.

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Things that are great with Mankind, as they are running all the time, in that they [ ... ]
chapters.note: No recoverable correspondential/cosmological substrate is present. The chapter is dominated by (a) hagiographic frame/self-attestation of Mani and (b) Christian overlay content about the name of Christ in ordinary piety (invocation, naming, oaths). The close shifts into heightened application/boasting but remains within the hagiographic voice rather than systematic cosmological exposition.

chapters.title: There is no Joy that shall remain in the World till the End.
chapters.note: Nearly the entire chapter is a compact, systematic cosmological exposition: the sun and moon cannot fully rejoice during the time of Mixture because (1) they behold the Enemy ruling, and (2) they behold the Living Soul oppressed until its final cleansing and the Enemy’s binding. Only the opening dialogue attribution is later frame material; there is no NT citation and no institutional/pastoral grafting.

chapters.title: Concerning the Form of the Word, that [ ... 30 ... ]
chapters.note: A compact, systematic five-fold correspondence teaching: the production of a word is analyzed through five mouth/throat members, then mirrored by a five-step artisan process (coin-making). Only the opening attribution is later frame; the teaching itself stays in impersonal, mechanical description without institutional application or NT overlay.

chapters.title: Concerning the Seed Grain that shall be formed by the Elements, and also be destroyed by them
chapters.note: Dominantly cosmological/process teaching using a seed-grain analogy: the five elements form/nourish, and the same cycle also entails deprivation/blight as Matter casts its shadow. Only paragraph 3 clearly pivots into institutional application (teachers/elect) while borrowing the analogy’s syntax.

chapters.title: Concerning the Fifty Lord's Days; to what Mysteries do they correspond? Or the Second (Fifty); to whose Sign (are they)?
chapters.note: The chapter opens with a late Q&A frame about catechumen/elect fasting. The oldest layer appears in the central computation-mapping: five garments × five powers → twenty-five limbs/sons, tied to the hypostases Summons/Answer/Obedience and the ascent mechanism. The second half shows strong editorial fatigue: institutional categories (catechumens/elect/church) and then explicit NT-derived narrative justifications (Christ’s desert fasting, Simon the leper, tomb), which are overlay/pastoral rather than substrate.

chapters.title: Concerning the Nourishment of the Person, for there are Powers in it [ ... / ... ]
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly technical and cosmological, describing the body as a purificatory mechanism (counts of seals/rulers; cleansing via voice/word/silence; expulsion and transmigration of dark powers). The only clear later material is a short hagiographic/dialogue opener in ¶1.

chapters.title: Concerning the Four Archetypes that occur in the Eye, and the Fifth that is hidden in them; to whom do they belong?
chapters.note: Highly fragmentary, but dominated by cosmological-correspondential teaching: elemental/cosmic attributions (Fire, Darkness/abyss, Light/living air) and a microcosm teaching on the eye/pupil tied to cosmic structure (cardinal points; First Man). Paragraphs 1 and 3 carry a light hagiographic dialogue frame (“Once again he speaks:”) and explanatory address that likely entered with the compilation frame, but the underlying exposition remains internal to the cosmic system (cosmos↔man correspondences) rather than institutional application.

chapters.title: The Human is less than all the Things of the Universe, and he is rebellious beyond them all.
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by hagiographic reminiscence (Mani-on-the-road scene) and polemical/ethical application against humanity’s blasphemy, followed by later catechetical lists (“five” and “three”). The oldest recoverable substrate appears only as embedded cosmological kernels (Light/Darkness mechanics; aeons; descent to the province of death; eschatological binding; Cross of Light as a cosmic presence).

chapters.title: The Chapter on whether any [Lig]ht comes from the Three Vessels.
chapters.note: This kephalaion is almost entirely systematic cosmological mechanism (gates, firmaments, rays, purification). The only clearly later material is the dialogue wrapper (“Once again…”, “The apostle says…”), which frames otherwise core teaching and a substantive cosmological question.

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Images that are in the righteous Person.
chapters.note: After a brief hagiographic opening, the chapter is largely a systematic, process-oriented exposition of a threefold inner structure (spiritual/psychic/corporeal) and the ascent/purification of the living soul through these degrees, culminating in the action of the Light Virgin/Virgin of Light. Only the final paragraph shows probable Christian-moral coloring (virtues; ‘first/last’ formula), while the main mechanism remains cosmological-anthropological rather than institutional/pastoral.

chapters.title: The Catechumen asks the Apostle: will Rest come about for Someone who has come out of the Body, if the Saints pray over and make an Alms-offering for him?
chapters.note: The chapter opens and closes in dialogue-frame and quickly pivots into two substantial archetypal “entreaty” narratives (Mother of Life → Living Spirit; then the Five → Third Ambassador) that are strongly cosmological and systematic (CORE). After these, the text drifts into church practice around alms/remembrance for the dead with heavy institutional vocabulary and a seam-flagged ecclesial extension (PASTORAL), consistent with the strong editorial-fatigue signal. A few late sections retain small embedded cosmological phrases (MIXED).

chapters.title: Concerning why if a [Nail] is cut the Person shall not be sick; but if a Limb is cut he shall immediately be pained.
chapters.note: This chapter is carried almost entirely by a dialogue frame (disciple question → apostle answer → closing reaction). The only recoverable older teaching substrate is the correspondential/analogical explanation in ¶5 (body~earth; limbs~trees; regrowing vs non-regrowing kinds). No NT overlay appears; the frame is hagiographic/compilational rather than Christian-citation.

chapters.title: Concerning why Some shall delay to come forth from the Body, and Others die in an instant.
chapters.note: This kephalaion is extremely fragmentary. Most surviving material is dialogue/request frame (¶1, ¶3, ¶4). Only ¶2 preserves non-framing instructional content about differing death/release timings; despite low register scores (likely due to lacunae suppressing detectable vocabulary), its voice and subject matter fit the older explanatory teaching layer.

Chapter 118 is almost entirely destroyed; only short fragments survive from ⟨p.283⟩–⟨p.284⟩. No clear hagiographic frame formulas, institutional/pastoral directives, or NT citation markers are preserved in the readable remnants. What survives is too lacunose to reconstruct sense, but the few legible cosmological terms (Light, universe, revealed) are most consistent with the teaching core.

chapters.title: Chapter 119
chapters.note: Core substrate survives mainly as a cosmological/hierarchical depiction of the First Man’s commissioning, steadfastness in the worlds of darkness, and the purifying/separating work against the Enemy. A later sermonic/pastoral layer intensifies in the second half (esp. ¶6, ¶9), turning the cosmology into direct exhortation and introducing church categories (notably “catechumen”) as an interpretive graft. No explicit NT citation formula appears; the Christian-sounding titles (“only begotten”, “righteous”) function here as internal honorifics rather than Gospel overlay.

chapters.title: Concerning the Two Essences
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by polemical address, moral examples, and Christianized/judgment language (strong application drift in the second half). The only clear recoverable substrate fragment is the bare cosmological axiom of the Two Essences (Light/Darkness) embedded in a hagiographic-looking frame sentence.

chapters.title: Concerning the Sect of the Basket
chapters.note: This kephalaion is front-loaded with hagiographic scene-setting and anti-sectarian/application material about “the basket” (¶1–4). The cosmological-teaching substrate appears only in the broken fragments of ¶5–6 (pillars, angels, cosmic supports, Living Spirit garments, Porter). ¶5 is especially unstable: a brief institutional phrase (“holy church”) intrudes into an otherwise cosmological enumeration, consistent with the chapter-level fatigue signal.

chapters.title: Concerning the 'Assent' and the 'Amen'
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by late liturgical/institutional application (assent/amen in congregational prayer, sealing, alms, healing, temptation among the elect), with only a small cosmological substrate explaining the divine archetypes (Summons/Obedience as "portals" redeeming the First Man). The editorial fatigue signal matches the text: after the initial cosmological explanation, the chapter drifts into church practice and exempla. A brief Christian/historical notice about "apostles" appears near the end.
